questions.q: Information disclosure is also known by what other name?
questions.explain: Information disclosure, also called information leakage, is when a website unintentionally reveals sensitive information to its users.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of information disclosure?
choices: Hidden directory names revealed through a robots.txt file or a directory listing
Database table or column names mentioned in an error message
API keys or database credentials hard-coded in source code
Small differences in application behavior that hint whether a username exists
Returning the same generic error message for every failed login
Serving every page over HTTPS
questions.explain: All of the first four appear in the material's list of examples. A generic error message is a recommended fix, and HTTPS has nothing to do with what the application itself reveals.

questions.q: Why can leaking purely technical information, such as framework names or directory structure, still be serious?
choices: It always lets an attacker read other users' data directly
It can open up more attack surface and provide the missing piece for a complex, high-severity attack
It automatically breaks the site's TLS encryption
Technical details are legally treated the same as credit card numbers
questions.explain: Technical details often have little direct impact on their own, but they can point to more attack surface or complete a chain toward a more serious exploit.

questions.q: Information disclosure usually happens while users are just browsing the site normally, and an attacker rarely has to do anything unusual to trigger it.
questions.explain: It occasionally happens during normal browsing, but more commonly the attacker has to interact with the site in unexpected or malicious ways and then study the responses closely.

questions.q: Developer comments left in HTML markup and visible in production fall into which category of cause?
choices: Insecure configuration of the website and related technologies
Flawed design and behavior of the application
Failure to remove internal content from public content
Weak cryptography
questions.explain: Forgotten developer comments are the material's example of internal content that was never removed from public content.

questions.q: A website shows overly verbose error messages because its default settings were never changed. Which category of cause is this?
choices: Insecure configuration of the website and related technologies
Failure to remove internal content from public content
Flawed design and behavior of the application
Insecure deserialization
questions.explain: Default configurations, and debugging or diagnostic features that were never turned off, both count as insecure configuration.

questions.q: A login form returns different responses depending on which error happened, which lets an attacker work out valid usernames. Which category of cause is this?
choices: Failure to remove internal content from public content
Flawed design and behavior of the application
Insecure configuration of the website and related technologies
Version control exposure
questions.explain: Returning distinct responses for different error states is a design flaw, and it allows enumeration of sensitive data such as valid credentials.

questions.q: According to the material, why is insecure configuration especially common?
choices: Web servers cannot be configured securely
Third-party technologies are widely used, and the people deploying them often don't fully understand their many configuration options
Browsers ignore server configuration
Configuration files are always publicly readable
questions.explain: Third-party technologies are everywhere, and their huge range of configuration options is not always well understood by the people setting them up.

questions.q: Information disclosure is usually a high-severity issue on its own.
questions.explain: It is high-severity on its own only in specific circumstances. Technical disclosure in particular matters mainly when you can show how an attacker could use it to do harm.

questions.q: A site reveals which framework version it uses. When does this become significant?
choices: Always, because any version information is critical
Only when the version is the latest release
When the version is old and has a known vulnerability, so a publicly documented exploit might work
Never, because version numbers are public anyway
questions.explain: Knowing the version of a fully patched framework is of limited use. It matters when that version has a known, publicly documented vulnerability.

questions.q: When you find potentially sensitive information being leaked, what should you mainly focus on?
choices: The fact that any disclosure exists at all
The impact and exploitability of the leaked information
How many bytes were leaked
Whether the information is shown in the page body or in a header
questions.explain: Minor technical details can be found on many sites. Focus on what the information lets an attacker do, unless the information is so sensitive that it deserves attention in its own right.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of information disclosure with a severe direct impact?
choices: Revealing which third-party framework a site uses
Revealing the directory structure
An online shop leaking its customers' credit card details
A fully patched server version shown in a header
questions.explain: Leaking highly sensitive user data such as credit card details is serious in itself. Framework names or directory structure usually have little direct impact.

questions.q: Which of the following are best practices for preventing information disclosure?
choices: Make sure everyone involved in building the site knows what information counts as sensitive
Audit code for information disclosure as part of QA or build processes
Use generic error messages as much as possible
Make sure debugging and diagnostic features are disabled in production
Learn the configuration of third-party technologies and disable features you don't need
List sensitive directories in robots.txt so they stay hidden
Show detailed stack traces so users can report bugs more easily
questions.explain: The first five are the recommended practices. Listing sensitive paths in robots.txt actually reveals them, and detailed stack traces are a classic source of leaks.

questions.q: Which disclosure-related task does the material describe as relatively easy to automate in a build process?
choices: Stripping developer comments
Rewriting business logic
Judging the severity of every possible leak
Training developers
questions.explain: Some audit tasks, such as stripping developer comments, can be automated as part of QA or the build.

questions.q: Preventing information disclosure completely is tricky because it can happen in a huge variety of ways.
questions.explain: Because it can happen in so many ways, the goal is to reduce the risk through general best practices.

questions.q: What does avoiding "tunnel vision" mean when testing for information disclosure?
choices: Testing only one page at a time
Not focusing too narrowly on one vulnerability, so you notice useful sensitive data wherever it shows up
Using only automated scanners
Ignoring error messages
questions.explain: Sensitive data can leak anywhere and is often found while testing for something else. A key skill is recognizing interesting information whenever you come across it.

questions.q: While fuzzing a parameter, which subtle clue besides the response content can reveal how the application behaves?
choices: A slight difference in the time taken to process the request
The color scheme of the page
The client's IP address
The browser's user agent
questions.explain: Responses can hint at behavior indirectly, for example through small timing differences.

questions.q: Even when an error message's content discloses nothing, the fact that one error case occurred instead of another can be useful information.
questions.explain: Which error case was reached reveals something about the application's internal logic.

questions.q: Which benefits of automating fuzzing with a tool like Burp Intruder does the material list?
choices: Adding payload positions to parameters and using pre-built wordlists of fuzz strings
Spotting differences in responses by comparing status codes, response times, lengths, and so on
Using grep match rules to flag keywords such as error, invalid, SELECT, or SQL
Using grep extraction rules to pull out and compare interesting items in responses
Automatically patching the vulnerabilities it finds
questions.explain: Intruder helps send and compare many inputs. It does not fix anything.

questions.q: What is Logger++?
choices: A built-in Burp Scanner check
A BApp Store extension that logs requests and responses from all Burp tools and supports advanced filters for highlighting interesting entries
A server-side logging library
A browser developer tools panel
questions.explain: Logger++ is an extension from the BApp Store, one of many that can help spot sensitive data leaked by a site.

questions.q: Which Burp edition includes Burp Scanner, which can automatically flag things like private keys, email addresses, credit card numbers, backup files, and directory listings?
choices: Burp Suite Community Edition
Burp Suite Professional
Any edition with Logger++ installed
None. It is a separate browser plugin
questions.explain: Burp Scanner is a Burp Suite Professional feature. It offers live scanning while you browse and scheduled automated crawl-and-audit scans.

questions.q: How do you open Burp's engagement tools?
choices: From the Intruder tab only
Right-click an HTTP message, a Proxy entry, or a site map item and choose "Engagement tools"
By installing them from the BApp Store
From a command-line flag at startup
questions.explain: The engagement tools are in the context menu of HTTP messages, Proxy entries, and site map items.

questions.q: Which Burp engagement tool helps find directories and files that are not linked from the site's visible content?
choices: Search
Find comments
Discover content
Logger++
questions.explain: Discover content finds content and functionality that won't necessarily appear in the site map on its own.

questions.q: Which advanced options does the engagement tools' Search feature offer for fine-tuning results?
choices: Regex search and negative search
Only exact case-sensitive matching
Search by HTTP status code only
Searching the server's file system
questions.explain: Regex and negative search let you quickly find where specific keywords appear, or where they are missing.

questions.q: What does the "Find comments" engagement tool do?
choices: Adds comments to the site's source code
Extracts developer comments from the selected item, with tabs showing the request/response in which each one was found
Finds user comments posted on blog pages
Removes comments from responses
questions.explain: It pulls out developer comments quickly and links each one back to the HTTP exchange where it appeared.

questions.q: In "engineering informative responses", what is one common approach the material describes?
choices: Waiting for the site to crash on its own
Making the application logic attempt an invalid action on a specific item of data, for example by submitting an invalid parameter value
Asking the site's administrators for logs
Clearing your browser cache
questions.explain: Watching how error messages change with your input, for example after an invalid parameter value, can produce stack traces or debug output, and sometimes reveals the desired data in the response.

questions.q: Which two files do many websites provide to help web crawlers navigate the site?
choices: /robots.txt
/sitemap.xml
/.htaccess
/index.php~
questions.explain: robots.txt and sitemap.xml often list directories that crawlers should skip, which can point to sensitive locations.

questions.q: Why might /robots.txt not show up in Burp's site map automatically?
choices: Burp blocks it by default
Such files usually aren't linked from within the website, so you may need to request them manually
It is only served over FTP
Browsers refuse to load it
questions.explain: Because crawler files are rarely linked from the site's pages, it is worth browsing to them directly.

questions.q: When can a web server automatically list a directory's contents?
choices: When the directory has no index page and the server is configured to list contents
Only when the directory is empty
Whenever HTTPS is disabled
Only for the root directory
questions.explain: Servers can be configured to auto-list directories that have no index page. This exposes resources such as temporary files and crash dumps.

questions.q: A directory listing is always a security vulnerability in itself.
questions.explain: It is not necessarily a vulnerability on its own. It becomes a clear issue when the site also lacks proper access control, so leaking where sensitive resources are matters.

questions.q: HTML developer comments are not visible on the rendered page. How can they still be viewed?
choices: Only with server access
Easily, using Burp or even the browser's built-in developer tools
Only by decompiling the browser
They cannot be viewed once deployed
questions.explain: Comments are part of the markup sent to the client, so anyone can read them with Burp or the browser's developer tools.

questions.q: A verbose error message names the template engine, database type, or server along with its version number. Why is that useful to an attacker?
choices: It lets them look up documented exploits, common misconfigurations, or dangerous defaults for that exact version
It reveals the administrator's password
It disables the site's error handling
It is not useful
questions.explain: Knowing the exact technology and version makes it easy to research known exploits and default-setting weaknesses. If the framework is open source, its public source code is also available to study.

questions.q: Observing differences between error messages is a key part of which techniques mentioned in the material?
choices: SQL injection and username enumeration
Clickjacking and CSRF
TLS downgrade attacks
Physical access attacks
questions.explain: Differences in error messages reveal behind-the-scenes behavior, which is central to techniques like SQL injection and username enumeration.

questions.q: Which kinds of information does the material say debug messages can contain?
choices: Values of key session variables that can be manipulated through user input
Hostnames and credentials for back-end components
File and directory names on the server
Keys used to encrypt data sent via the client
Passwords saved in the visitor's browser
questions.explain: These four come from the server side. The visitor's browser-saved passwords are not part of the application's debug output.

questions.q: A site loads account data with GET /user/personal-info?user=carlos. The page itself is protected, but the code that fetches the email address doesn't check that the user parameter matches the logged-in user. What is the result?
choices: Nothing, because the full page is protected
Changing the user parameter can show other users' email addresses on the attacker's own account page
The server crashes
Only the attacker's own email address can ever be shown
questions.explain: Weak logic for loading individual data items can leak other users' data. This connects to access control and IDOR vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Why does requesting a referenced .php file usually not reveal its source code?
choices: PHP files are encrypted
The server executes code in files with that extension instead of sending the file as text
Browsers block .php downloads
PHP source is always stored offsite
questions.explain: Servers execute files with handled extensions. A temporary backup copy with a different name or extension may not be executed, and its contents may be returned instead.

questions.q: Which character do text editors often append to a filename to mark a temporary backup file?
questions.explain: Backup files are often marked with a trailing tilde (~) or a different file extension.

questions.q: Which vulnerability does the material name as one that becomes much easier to find and exploit once source code is available?
choices: Insecure deserialization
Clickjacking
Open redirect
DNS rebinding
questions.explain: Access to source code can expose vulnerabilities like insecure deserialization that would otherwise be almost impossible to find.

questions.q: If the HTTP TRACE method is enabled, what does the server do, and how can that cause information disclosure?
choices: It returns the server's source code
It echoes the exact request it received, which can reveal things like internal authentication headers added by reverse proxies
It lists all users
It deletes the requested resource
questions.explain: TRACE is a diagnostic method. The echoed request can include headers that intermediaries added, such as the names of internal authentication headers.

questions.q: By default, what folder does a Git project store its version control data in?
questions.explain: If a site exposes its .git directory in production, it may be reachable just by browsing to /.git.

questions.q: Downloading an exposed .git directory always gives you the website's full source code.
questions.explain: It might not include the full source. Opening it with a local Git install shows the history and logs, and the diffs reveal snippets of code that may contain hard-coded sensitive data.
